method:
I began by reviewing Giddings’s archival documents and extracting key terms, which served as the foundation for conceptualizing my Week 4 project.
Concurrently, I consulted Ryan regarding technical approaches for converting 2D imagery into 3D. He suggested several methods: photogrammetry (creating 3D models from smartphone photos); CGI reconstruction based on historical photographs (a reference to someone named Victor Vergan/Bergen—name to be verified); and AI-driven 3D scene generation from photos, as developed by Fei-Fei Li’s team (also to be verified). We also discussed the principles of Renaissance-era perspective and the "illusion of depth" created by binocular vision.

Reading: The instructor’s new book (the lecture mentions that a QR code is available for online access, and a link is also provided on Blackboard). The title was not explicitly stated in the transcript; it is noted as *Why Look at Toys* in the Week 3 notes—this remains to be verified.
ludic: Relating to play or games; playful.
articulated: Having movable joints (e.g., a doll with bendable legs).
imaginative agency: The capacity to exercise initiative within imaginative play—a power shared among children, objects, and technology.
open-ended toy vs. game: An open-ended toy (lacking fixed rules or a win/loss outcome) contrasted with a game (defined by specific rules and a win/loss structure).
hybrid play: Play that combines physical objects with digital screens (e.g., *Skylanders*, *Amiibo*).
Internet of Toys: A category of toys that saw significant investment in the mid-2010s but ultimately proved unsuccessful.

Works: Ge Yulu’s "Fake Street Sign" project; *The Naked City* (Situationist International); *Amsterdam Real Time*; Buckminster Fuller’s Dymaxion map; Jasper Johns’s Dymaxion-themed paintings; *Beauty Earth* (Minecraft); Yoko Ono’s *Map Piece*; On Kawara’s *I Went* / *I Got Up* / *Today* / *42nd Parallel*; a project concerning rivers in Taiwan (by Su Yuxin—to be verified).
Figures: Buckminster Fuller, Gerardus Mercator, Jasper Johns, Yoko Ono, On Kawara, Kasper König (recipient of the postcards), John Dos Passos, Victor Bergen/Vergan (to be verified), Li Fei-Fei (to be verified).
Reading: A book by Jonathan Crary on the technologies of the observer (referenced in the text as "Technology of the Observer"—likely *Techniques of the Observer*; a Chinese translation exists—to be verified).
conclusion_future_work:
I am considering whether the inspiration drawn from all of this can be applied to my final project, while also reflecting on whether the various techniques and modes of thought I am currently using might be adapted and extended to other works, given the constraints I am working under.

Week Project：write about and/or make some work predicated on technology, art and maps.
results_discussion:
1. Technology as toys, not tools (0:01:53–0:25): A thought experiment—stone axes and spears may have first emerged through "play." Evidence: In ancient Egypt and Aztec civilization, wheeled toys appeared before functional wheeled vehicles; the wheel was first used for ritual purposes before being adopted for transporting goods. Toys possess three technical characteristics: scale (sized to fit a child’s hands), tactility (can be held or squeezed), and operability (can be manipulated or set in motion).
2. Toys vs. games (0:25–0:47): *Snakes and Ladders* is a "game" (defined by strict rules and a clear win/loss outcome). Will Wright, the designer of *SimCity*, describes his creation as a "software toy"—there is no winning or losing, allowing users to explore and invent their own ways to play. In digital games, while the user’s fingers do not physically touch the objects, the in-game characters exhibit their own "autonomous behaviors."
3. Insights for designers (from 0:47, expanded during the Q&A): The tension between "play" and "games" can help clarify how users interact with your work. The speaker’s advice: When designing interactive projects—whether "serious" or "playful"—you must ask yourself: How much openness and flexibility do you want to provide, and to what extent do you intend to direct the user's activity?

1. Opening: Ge Yu Road (0:00–0:07) — An artist installed an unauthorized street sign in Beijing’s Chaoyang District, naming the "road" after himself. The project began in 2013; by 2015, the road had been incorporated into official government records and digital maps. It gained widespread fame following his 2017 graduation exhibition, even appearing on CCTV. The instructor poses a question: at what moment did the name become "reality"? The answer lies in how maps and official systems transformed a fiction into a fact.
2. Psychogeography (0:07–0:14) — Maps created by the Situationist International. These works—likely a reference to Guy Debord’s 1957 *The Naked City*—overlay a standard map of Paris with red lines tracing the emotional contours of a *dérive* (drift). Here, the map shifts from being "neutral and objective" to representing "subjective experience"; the act of drifting serves as a record of time.
3. Real-time Trajectories (0:14–0:17) — *Amsterdam Real Time*: Dozens of participants carried GPS devices while commuting to work or school, effectively mapping the shape of Amsterdam through their movements. The instructor links this to the concept of "chronophotography" (discussed the previous week), where actions unfolding over time are translated into spatial information.
4. Altering Projections (0:17–0:31) —
*   The Mercator projection (1569) preserves angles but causes severe distortion near the poles; in contrast, Buckminster Fuller’s Dymaxion map (designed in 1943, patented in 1946) depicts the world’s landmasses as a single, interconnected archipelago. 
*   Jasper Johns utilized the Dymaxion map in his paintings, though with a different—more pessimistic and ambiguous—intent, demonstrating how the same map can convey divergent perspectives. 
*   In 2020, the *Minecraft* project "Beauty Earth" explored various projections for the game’s flat world map. After comparing the Mercator, equirectangular, and Dymaxion projections, the team opted to manually segment and rotate the map to preserve directional orientation. 5. Maps as Evidence and Narrative (0:28–0:43):
Yoko Ono’s *Map Piece*: Draw an imaginary map, follow it, and if the path is blocked, forge your own way.
On Kawara: *I Went* (12 small map-based booklets), *I Got Up* (postcards sent to recipients, noting the time he woke up), and his *Today* series (paintings of dates).
The 1968 *42nd Parallel* mail art project: Postcards were sent along the 42nd parallel north, tracing a circuit across the United States—a "slow" medium countering "fast" media (the instructor contextualizes this within the same era as Apollo 7 and the launch of *Dong Fang Hong I*).
Related literary work: John Dos Passos’s *U.S.A.* trilogy (exact title in the transcript is unclear; requires verification).
6. River-themed works by a Taiwanese artist (0:35–0:43; transcript provides the phonetic name "Su Yuxin"—requires verification): A project concerning a river in Taipei that was filled in to become a road. The work presents three layers of maps side-by-side: a map from the Japanese colonial period, an aerial photograph taken by the U.S. military, and a contemporary Google Map. Maps serve as imagery of state power; meanwhile, Google Maps navigation can transform into a cinematic space that facilitates "time travel."
7. Discussion (0:45–0:57):
The instructor notes that while maps appear "indexical" (pointing directly to reality), they are actually a "suturing" together of various technologies—yet we accept them as absolute truth.
Maps "make the territory"; the act of mapping is an exercise of power.
"Counter-mapping": The practice of creating maps by those who lack institutional voice, such as women or colonized peoples.
A participant points out that following a map could lead one straight off a cliff; the very "trust" we place in maps is something that should be questioned.
title: Presentations by the two guests—Seth Giddings＆Chinese doctoral students at this university
introduction:
Seth Giddings, Professor of Ludic Technologies, argues that technology can function first as a toy and subsequently as a tool. He distinguishes toys from games, noting that toys are open-ended—lacking defined win or loss conditions—and rely on manual engagement and imagination. A question for designers of creative technologies: to what extent do you want your users to experience openness and freedom, versus being guided through the process?
Creative / Digital Mapping: Maps are more than just spatial media; they also possess a temporal dimension. Maps can record reality, and in turn, reshape it. Yet, maps are imbued with power—even as they often lead us to mistakenly perceive them as "objective."
